analysis.one_liner: Permanently lets U.S. banks and insurers defer American taxes on profits earned through overseas financing arms.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died without a vote when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax rules, when a U.S. company earns certain kinds of foreign income through an overseas subsidiary, the parent company owes U.S. tax on it right away. This bill would permanently exempt income from banking, financing, and insurance businesses from that rule, letting financial firms keep their foreign profits abroad without paying U.S. tax until they bring the money home. The exemption was temporary under the law at the time; this bill would remove its expiration date.
analysis.who_benefits: American banks, finance companies, and insurance companies with foreign operations, which could indefinitely defer U.S. tax on profits from their overseas financing businesses. The tax would only come due if and when the earnings were returned to the U.S. parent, so firms could keep the money offshore and reinvest it tax-free.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and insurers with foreign arms

how_it_helps.text: Allows American financial services firms doing business abroad to defer U.S. tax on their foreign banking, financing, and insurance earnings until those earnings are returned to the U.S. parent company.

Removes the expiration dates on the temporary subpart F exemptions for active financing income and exempt insurance income, making the deferral benefit permanent for tax years beginning after December 31, 2001.
Attracted bipartisan support: 47 House members from both parties signed on as cosponsors.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers, who forgo the tax revenue that would otherwise be collected on financial firms' foreign profits. Non-financial companies earning similar foreign income would not get the same break, leaving the benefit concentrated in the financial sector.

drawbacks.text: Shrinks federal revenue by letting financial firms defer U.S. tax indefinitely on foreign profits, a cost that falls on the Treasury and taxpayers at large.
The benefit goes only to banking, financing, and insurance businesses, not to other companies or to individuals, so it carves out a permanent advantage for one sector.
Deferral encourages keeping earnings offshore: the tax is only triggered when profits are brought back to the U.S. parent, so firms have a standing incentive to reinvest abroad rather than at home.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the financial companies involved, the benefit is real and durable: indefinite tax deferral on foreign profits is worth a great deal. For everyone else, the bill offers nothing directly, while reducing federal revenue and favoring one sector of business over all others. There is no provision that lowers anyone's tax bill at home or funds any public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2001 by Rep. Jim McCrery and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
It gathered 47 cosponsors from both parties, including 32 Republicans and 15 Democrats.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the House never voted, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and ordinary taxpayers are better off, since no tax deferral for financial firms became law. Financial companies did not lose out permanently, though: Congress later enacted the same active financing exemption as a temporary provision, so the idea stayed alive.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the exemption never became law

for.name: Jim McCrery
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-LA), bill sponsor and Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 colleagues to join as original cosponsors.

for.name: 32 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Ways and Means members such as Camp, Crane, Dunn, English, Herger, Houghton, Hulshof, Johnson of Connecticut, Ramstad, Ryan of Wisconsin, Shaw, and Weller.

for.name: 15 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Ways and Means members Neal of Massachusetts, Matsui, McDermott, Pomeroy, Kleczka, McNulty, and Tanner.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or scheduled it for floor action; the bill sat with no committee action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 32 Republicans and 15 Democrats cosponsored, and the bill stalled in committee rather than failing on any party-line vote.

industries.industry: U.S. banks and finance companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The bill gives these firms permanent tax deferral on profits from overseas financing arms, cutting the taxes they owe the U.S. government, possibly forever if profits stay offshore. The revenue foregone is a cost borne by everyone else, and no comparable break is offered to other taxpayers.
The bill permanently exempts income from foreign insurance subsidiaries from immediate U.S. taxation under the same deferral scheme, a benefit limited to insurers that operate abroad.
